source: Kulkarni & Simon (1987/1988) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation (CMU tech report AIP-5; journal version Cognitive Science 12(2):139-175)
finding: First-hand read of KEKADA. It is a production system built from Holmes's reconstruction of Krebs's urea-cycle work (Jul 1931 to Apr 1932). Its heuristics are grouped into problem-choosers, problem-generators, decision-makers, experiment-proposers, expectation-setters, experimenters, hypothesis-generators/modifiers, confidence-modifiers and hypothesis/strategy-choosers. Each hypothesis carries a confidence record: success, failure, failed-effort, implied-success, implied-failure.
numbers: Heuristic table (Fig 4-1): 31 domain-independent and 33 domain-specific heuristics (64 total). By group, domain-independent/specific: problem choosers 9/0, problem generators 1/0, decision makers 4/6, experiment proposers 3/5, expectation setters 4/0, hypothesis generators 3/5, hypothesis modifiers 2/16, confidence modifiers 3/2, strategy choosers 2/0 (counts as printed in an OCR scan). Only one problem-generator rule exists (PG1).
quote: The outcomes of experiments are supplied interactively by the user.
limits: Tech-report text from an OCR scan. The DOI given earlier in this folder (cog1202_4) belongs to a different 1988 paper (Sweller); the right DOI is 10.1207/s15516709cog1202_1. Experiment outcomes are NOT simulated: the user types them in (heuristic E1). Holmes's book itself was still not opened.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete, small operator vocabulary: set expectation, run, compare, and if outside bounds raise a puzzle task with top priority. This is the only primary operator list we hold.

source: Kulkarni & Simon (1987/1988) KEKADA: surprise rule and choosers
finding: The surprise mechanism is explicit. ES1 sets an expected value from earlier runs with lower and upper bounds plus a tolerance. PG1: if an outcome violates expectations, make the puzzling phenomenon a task. PC8: a new puzzle task beats all other tasks. Hypothesis priority order (DM9) is predefined: (1) a known stimulant may be necessary, (2) divide and conquer, (3) scope of the phenomenon, (4) others. Hypotheses are made inactive after a set number of failed experiments or failed effort (HM4, HM5).
numbers: Generators: HG1 'a class of substances shows the same outcome' (scope), HG2 'a missing substance causes the low output', HG3 divide and conquer on subprocesses, HG5 'an intermediate exists', HG7 mixed versus additive action. Experiment proposers EP1-EP8. Thresholds in the 1987 report are 'a specified high value' with no number given.
limits: The authors say the predefined order DM9 is a stand-in for Krebs's unknown prior experience, and that some choices were left to the user (DM10). Rules are hand-written, not learned.
agent_relevance: A direct template for a surprise check: expectation with bounds, a violation test, a puzzle task that pre-empts the plan, then a fixed order of explanations (known factor, split into parts, scope).

source: Kulkarni & Simon (1987/1988) KEKADA simulation log of the ornithine-cycle discovery
finding: Run narrative: pick urea synthesis (PC1-7), test alanine alone, ammonia alone and both. Alanine gave less urea than the lower bound, a surprise, which triggered 3 explanations (missing substance in the tissue slice, a subprocess defect, a class of substances). The missing-substance idea was tried with glucose and fructose and failed; the subprocess idea re-confirmed known facts; the class idea led to testing amino acids until ornithine, which with ammonia gave about double the ammonia-only rate, a second surprise. Then scope tests found no other substance with the effect, then a catalyst test (25 molecules of urea per ornithine in the simulation; 24.5 in Krebs's April 13 experiment), then the citrulline intermediate.
numbers: Authors' fit claim: 'only minor differences' between the program's course and Krebs's. This is stated, not measured. No count of experiments is reported for the simulated run. Real chronology: first experiment Jul 26 1931; ornithine effect Nov 15; scope phase mid-Nov to mid-Jan; reaction path Jan 14 to Apr 13.
limits: Hand-crafted to fit one case; the user supplies results and some choices (INT), so the run shows sufficiency of the rules, not that they would find it blind. The glutamine rerun is a second case by the same authors.
agent_relevance: Two surprises in a row, each hijacking the plan, is the pattern. Our agent should be able to re-plan twice, not once.

source: Kulkarni & Simon (1990) Experimentation in Machine Discovery (NASA Ames tech report FIA-90-09-24-02)
finding: KEKADA control rule stated plainly: normally it loops over hypotheses and their experiments (breadth-first); when a result is surprising it drops its earlier goals and works only on the new phenomenon, which is depth-first without backtracking. Five domain-independent strategies: magnification, scope, divide and conquer, factor analysis (remove one entity at a time), and relating two anomalies that share a variable. Second case: glutamine synthesis from 'ornithine produces ammonia in kidney'. Magnification (vary apparatus variables) failed first, scope tests were done next (4 amino acids needed to generalise), then a glutamic acid surprise, then an arsenite surprise, then glutamine.
numbers: Scope thresholds: more than 3 members with the effect generalises the claim; more than 3 without it inactivates the hypothesis. The given starting surprise was followed by 2 surprises found by the run (glutamic acid rate, arsenite) before the glutamine reaction; the paper tabulates knowledge states S1-S5.
quote: this counterintuitive strategy works quite well in the scientific domains we have examined
limits: Again user-supplied results. The paper calls the surprise-chasing 'counterintuitive' but says it 'works quite well in the scientific domains we have examined'; two cases only, no baseline without the surprise rule.
agent_relevance: Gives a loop to copy: threshold of 3 for scope, magnify first, drop old goals on surprise. The missing piece is an ablation (see d18).

source: Holmes's Krebs chronology as summarised in Kulkarni & Simon (1988), sections 1.2.1-1.2.3
finding: Counts of time stuck and of method changes for Krebs. About 16 weeks (Jul 26 to Nov 15 1931) passed before the first surprise. Inside that: about 4 weeks re-verifying known facts about urea from ammonia, then amino acids tested against ammonia (alanine, phenylalanine, glycine, cysteine, cystine) with only negative results, then a switch in the first two weeks of November to glucose, fructose, lactate and citrate with no hypothesis, then the ornithine test on Nov 15. After the surprise: about 8.5 weeks (to mid-Jan 1932) of scope testing that found the effect specific to ornithine, then new apparatus Jan 14 and ammonia confirmed as the nitrogen source by Jan 23, then catalyst experiments in March, 24.5 urea per ornithine on Apr 13, citrulline tested Apr 25, paper appeared Apr 30.
numbers: Method changes visible in the record: (1) known-fact checking to amino-acid sweep, (2) amino-acid sweep to carbohydrate-intermediate sweep, (3) test of ornithine (cause disputed: Krebs said availability, Holmes suggested it was an unsolved metabolic problem), (4) scope sweep to mechanism, (5) new apparatus. That is about 5 shifts in 8.5 months. 3.5 months to the key phenomenon and about 5 more months to test and interpret.
limits: A single case, told second-hand through K&S, not from Holmes's own text or the notebooks. 'Impasse' is the reader's label: the sources describe negative results and a change of line, not a stated feeling of being stuck.
agent_relevance: This is the first dated count we have: roughly one method change every 7 weeks, and the winning move was an off-plan test after many negative results. Supports a rule like 'after N negative sweeps, run an off-plan probe'.

source: Kepler's Mars work, Astronomia nova (Wikipedia summary of Kepler's own statements)
finding: Kepler wrote that his iterative method for the vicarious hypothesis needed 'at least seventy repetitions of it, at a very great loss of time'. He tried the vicarious hypothesis, bisected eccentricity and an oval orbit, built an ellipse-based construction with an error, and wrote that he 'laid it aside, and fell back on ellipses'. Work began by 1602, the manuscript was done by Sept 1607, published Aug 1609.
numbers: At least 70 repetitions of one computation; about 5.5 years from start to manuscript; 4 named model families tried.
quote: I laid it aside, and fell back on ellipses.
limits: Tertiary source (Wikipedia). The page gives no total count of trials before the ellipse. This is a count of one subroutine, not of method changes. Hanson versus Lugg is not tested by it.
agent_relevance: A rare example of a measured amount of failed search in a famous case; it shows a long grind with a return to an earlier rejected idea (ellipse), which a loop with memory of dropped ideas must allow.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench, Fig 4 left (read in raw text mode to untangle the table)
finding: Clean table recovered, replacing the garbled reading in critique item 2. Hypothesis Matching Score (HMS), columns GPT-4o / GPT-4p / Llama-3-70B. DB-REAL: NoDataGuess 0.0 / 4.7 / 11.5; CodeGen 15.5 / 16.3 / 12.1; ReAct 15.4 / 15.6 / 13.5; DataVoyager 15.4 / 13.9 / 11.5; Reflexion (Oracle) 24.5 / 19.5 / 22.5. DB-SYNTH: CodeGen 14.1 / 8.7 / 10.9; ReAct 11.6 / 7.4 / 12.0; DataVoyager 5.7 / 6.9 / 11.7; Reflexion (Oracle) 15.7 / 12.9 / 23.2.
numbers: Memory effect: the no-data guess is 0% of the CodeGen score for GPT-4o (0.0 vs 15.5), 29% for GPT-4p (4.7 vs 16.3) and 95% for Llama-3 (11.5 vs 12.1). ReAct minus CodeGen on DB-REAL: -0.1, -0.7, +1.4. DataVoyager minus CodeGen: -0.1, -2.4, -0.6. On DB-SYNTH DataVoyager GPT-4o is 5.7 vs CodeGen 14.1. The 25% best is Reflexion with an oracle (24.5), not a normal agent; best non-oracle is 16.3.
limits: Row assignment checked against the text (GPT-4o 'refuses to hallucinate' in NoDataGuess = 0.0; 'Llama-3 performs similarly in both modes' = 11.5 vs 12.1; ReAct and DataVoyager 'do not help'). Read from PDF raw text, not from an image of the figure. One run per cell, no confidence intervals given.
agent_relevance: Corrects K20 and K05: the memory effect is large only for Llama-3, near zero for GPT-4o. The 'best 25%' in K05 needs the oracle label. Extra reasoning prompts gave no gain over plain code writing.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench Table 1 and Fig 4 text
finding: Exact no-data (DataBlind) versus data-driven (LLM-SR) symbolic accuracy on LSR-Transform: Llama-3.1-8B 3.61 vs 30.63; GPT-3.5-turbo 2.10 vs 10.81; GPT-4o-mini 7.21 vs 31.53. Figure 4 compares original Feynman and transformed forms at equal tree size (averaged over all method-LLM pairs) and the text says transformed problems are 'substantially more challenging', also in the 0-15 node band.
numbers: Figure 4 plotted values are NOT in the PDF text, so the original-versus-transformed gap in points could not be read. Only the direction is quoted. Table 1 gives the DataBlind numbers above.
quote: substantially more challenging for current discovery methods than original Feynman problems
limits: Gap 3 (Figure 4 magnitude) stays open: reading the plot needs the image or the authors' data. Averages are over methods and LLMs, so they mix strong and weak cells.
agent_relevance: Data access multiplies symbolic accuracy about 4x to 8x at the small-model end. Our check: always compare a with-data run to a no-data run on the same item.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench, appendix E.1 (DataBlind on LSR-Transform and on NewtonBench)
finding: The memory effect on LSR-Transform has grown with newer models. DataBlind symbolic accuracy: GPT-3.5-turbo 2.10, Llama-3.1-8b 3.61, GPT-4o-mini 7.21 (the first three from the original paper); Nemotron-ultra-253b 28.83, Kimi-K2 30.63, Qwen-3-next 33.33, o4-mini 34.23, GPT-4.1 35.14. On NewtonBench the no-data score is 0 for GPT-4o-mini, Nemotron-ultra-253b and GPT-4.1, with or without a hint that the law is shifted.
numbers: Rise from 2.10-7.21 to 28.83-35.14 (about 5x to 17x) between model generations on the same 111 items. Counterfactual shift items: 0 of 3 models score anything blind.
limits: Three models only on NewtonBench, authors' own control. The o4-mini example shows the model deriving the transformed form from the textbook law, which is derivation from memory, not recall of the same string.
agent_relevance: LSR-Transform no longer blocks recall for strong models, so rediscovery scores on 'obscured' forms can still be inflated. Counterfactual laws are the safer test.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench appendix B.2: GPT-4o as symbolic-equivalence judge
finding: The only human check of the judge: two of the authors independently judged 130 randomly sampled problems; GPT-4o agreed with them in 123 of 130 (94.6%).
numbers: 123/130 = 94.6% raw agreement. No chance-corrected figure (kappa), no split into false accepts and false rejects, no breakdown by method.
limits: Raters are authors; the share of 'equivalent' cases in the 130 is not given, so 94.6% could be close to chance if most cases are one class. Constants are replaced by placeholders before judging, so a form with wrong structure but right fit is judged on form only.
agent_relevance: Judge agreement is good on equation equivalence, a narrow, checkable task. It does not transfer to judging a prose hypothesis. Use a code-side algebra check beside the judge.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: grading of discovered knowledge, human versus agent
finding: Task completion and the procedure score are automatic. The explanatory-knowledge score uses binary questions graded by GPT-4o for the agents. For the human scientists the notes were instead graded manually on a 0 / 0.5 / 1 scale. No agreement figure between GPT-4o and a human grader is reported.
numbers: Humans: 11 scientists, 16 tasks, seed 0 only, normal and challenge settings only; completion 66%, knowledge 55%. Agent knowledge scores come from the GPT-4o binary questions.
limits: The two graders use different scales and different material (agent memory structures vs free-form notes), so the human-versus-agent knowledge gap is not like for like. A code-only check cannot see the knowledge score at all.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a headline knowledge gap without a human-graded sample of agent output. Plan to grade 30-50 of our own outputs by hand to measure judge error.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld Tables 4 and 5: where the agents fail, and what the unit tests really are
finding: Corrects K06. The ten unit tests are generic skills (dialog, pick-and-place, measuring with an instrument, door and key navigation, search), not the stages of discovery. Average unit-test completion is 0.60 (ReAct), 0.44 (Plan+Execute) and 0.64 (Hypothesizer); several navigation tests are at 0.00-0.20. So '60%+ on parts' mostly shows basic world skills, not discovery sub-skills. Per theme, agents do the work but fail to conclude: procedure scores are high and completion low (Proteomics Easy ReAct procedure 0.87, completion 0.20; Normal 0.88/0.40).
numbers: Reactor Lab regression (curve fitting): completion 0.00 for all 3 agents at all 3 difficulties (9 cells) while procedure is 0.38-0.51. Easy-level averages ReAct procedure 0.59, completion 0.38, knowledge 0.25; Hypothesizer 0.56, 0.28, 0.34. Challenge: ReAct 0.63, 0.18, 0.10; Hypothesizer 0.49, 0.08, 0.08. 5 seeds per cell, GPT-4o for all agents.
limits: Five seeds per cell, one model. The failure location (fitting and concluding, not acting) is inferred from score columns, not from labelled traces.
agent_relevance: Independent evidence for gap 7: in this benchmark the agents run the experiments but do not turn data into a fitted relation. Interpretation, not action, is where the score is lost, which fits Kosmos (d13).

source: Mitchener et al. (2025) Kosmos: breakdown of statement accuracy, and the leak control
finding: Accuracy of 102 statements from 3 reports, judged by expert scientists: 79.4% overall; 85.5% for data-analysis statements; 82.1% for literature statements; 57.9% for synthesis (interpretation) statements. Authors read the gap as a tendency to confuse statistically significant with scientifically valuable results. For one rediscovery (Piazza et al. preprint, neuron morphology) they reran with models whose cutoff is before the preprint and still got the lognormal and scaling findings.
numbers: 85.5 / 82.1 / 57.9 per type; 102 statements; 3 reports; pre-cutoff rerun reproduced both findings. Runs are stochastic and 'multiple independent runs may not consistently converge on the same discoveries'.
limits: Evaluators are collaborators of the authors, not blind outside raters; only 3 reports. The pattern 'interpretation is worst' now has two sources (Kosmos, DiscoveryWorld) from different teams, but there is no independent audit of Kosmos.
agent_relevance: Interpretation is the weak step across two systems: add an explicit check that separates 'significant' from 'meaningful'. The pre-cutoff rerun is a cheap leak control we can copy.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Co-Scientist: the cf-PICI rediscovery as reported
finding: The paper reports a single run: asked how capsid-forming PICIs (cf-PICIs) spread across species, the system proposed, in two days, a top-ranked hypothesis that they interact with diverse phage tails, matching the group's then-unpublished, co-timed result. The authors call it a recapitulation. In the text I read there is no replication, no repeated runs, no count of the other hypotheses proposed, and no leak control (such as a model with an earlier cutoff).
numbers: n = 1 case; 2 days; the goal text itself already names the cf-PICI question ('how the same cf-PICI can be found in different bacterial species'). Compare Kosmos, which did report a pre-cutoff rerun for its rediscovery (d13).
limits: I found no independent replication or leak audit, but the search tools were down, so one may exist that I could not find. Absence here means 'not in the source', not 'does not exist'.
agent_relevance: Treat the cf-PICI result as an anecdote with a prior-knowledge risk. Gap 9 stays open.

source: Shi et al. (2026) The Weight of Teamwork: scope and limits of the sampling result
finding: Re-read for scope. The comparison is call-matched (50 scheduled calls per problem), not token-matched, and the paper says so. The base is a 7B model (qwen2.5-7b-instruct, temperature 0.7, 512-token cap; a second layer used a GPT-5-family model with no reasoning). The comparison is independent trajectories versus one long 50-call chain and versus peer-visible topologies, not versus structured scaffolds with tools. Each prompt shows only 5 training rows.
numbers: Setups (agents x rounds): 1x50, 2x25, 5x10, 10x5, all 50 calls. 100 Qwen problems (50 Transform, 50 Synth); 41 Transform problems in the GPT layer. Selection rule matters: Complete minus Independent was +0.10 under archive-wide selection and -0.75 under final-round selection. 9 of 20 prespecified interactions survived Holm correction. Bootstrap is over problems; no repeat over sampling seeds.
limits: Single preprint, no seed replication, no equal-token control, symbolic regression only. The authors say the communication mechanism is not identified and that results do not mean multi-agent work should be avoided.
agent_relevance: Weakens K09: the claim that independent sampling beats talking holds for a weak model with five data rows at equal calls. It does not test our scaffold. Run our own equal-token test.

source: Tran & Kiela (2026) Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets
finding: Closest outside support for the equal-compute idea (abstract read; full text not opened). Across Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama and Gemini 2.5, single agents match or beat several multi-agent designs when reasoning tokens are held equal on multi-hop reasoning. They report budget-control artifacts (especially the Gemini 2.5 API) and benchmark artifacts that inflate multi-agent gains. Multi-agent becomes competitive when single-agent context use is degraded or compute is larger.
numbers: Three model families; numbers not read. Not a discovery task and not a test of independent sampling.
limits: Abstract only. Different task (multi-hop QA), so it supports 'equal tokens matter' and not 'sampling beats scaffolds on discovery'.
agent_relevance: Supports our rule to compare at equal tokens and to check how tokens are counted (API budget artifacts).

source: Kim et al. (2025/2026) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
finding: Controlled study across 260 configurations, six agent benchmarks, five architectures (single plus Independent, Centralized, Decentralized, Hybrid multi-agent) and three LLM families, with tools, prompts and compute standardised. Gains from coordination shrink once the single-agent baseline is strong; tool-heavy tasks pay multi-agent overhead; architectures without central verification spread errors more.
numbers: Cross-validated R^2 = 0.373 (0.413 with a task-grounded capability metric). Change versus single agent runs from +80.8% (decomposable financial reasoning) to -70.0% (sequential planning). Picks the best architecture for 87% of held-out configurations.
limits: Abstract read only; the six benchmarks are not discovery tasks and Shi et al. note that the capability threshold did not transfer in leave-one-domain-out tests. Authorship (Kim, Yubin et al.) matched to Shi's citation by topic, not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Task shape decides if structure helps: decomposable work gains, sequential work loses. Discovery is sequential and stateful, so default to a single loop plus parallel independent samples.

source: What could not be closed in this pass: tool and access log
finding: The shared web-search quota was used up; arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex search endpoints returned 429 or no budget. Wiley, DTIC and ResearchGate pages returned 403 or a bot check. Direct arXiv PDFs, archive.org downloads, Crossref and Wikipedia worked. So no search for (a) an ablation of mined operator sequences, (b) an LLM surprise-detection rate study, (c) a measured Hanson-versus-Lugg comparison, or (d) a cf-PICI replication could be run.
numbers: Searches attempted: 8 arXiv queries (rate limited), 1 web search (refused), plus Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex (429 / no budget).
limits: A null here is a tool limit, not evidence of absence. Gaps 2, 6 (rate), 9 (replication) and 10 stay open for a rerun when search budget returns.
agent_relevance: Rerun these four searches first on the next pass.
